introduction: The High Court enjoys a very wide range of powers. It is a court of record, has the power of judicial review, and exercises administrative control over all subordinate courts within its territorial jurisdiction.

core_concepts.title: Original Jurisdiction
core_concepts.description: It means the power of a High Court to hear disputes in the first instance. This includes matters of marriage, divorce, company laws, contempt of court, and disputes relating to the election of MPs and MLAs.

core_concepts.title: Writ Jurisdiction (Article 226)
core_concepts.description: The High Court can issue writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, etc.) for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights AND for any other legal right. This makes the HC's writ jurisdiction wider than that of the Supreme Court.

core_concepts.title: Supervisory Jurisdiction (Article 227)
core_concepts.description: The High Court has the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals functioning within its territorial jurisdiction (except military courts or tribunals).

core_concepts.title: Court of Record (Article 215)
core_concepts.description: The judgments of the High Court are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony. These are admitted as evidentiary value in subordinate courts and cannot be questioned. It also has the power to punish for its own contempt.

important_entities.name: Article 226
important_entities.significance: This is a frequent exam topic because it allows the High Court to protect not just fundamental rights but also ordinary legal rights.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: UPSC favorite trap: The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction (Art 32) is narrower than the High Court's (Art 226) because the SC can only issue writs for Fundamental Rights, whereas the HC can issue them for 'any other purpose' (legal rights).
High Courts have NO power of superintendence over military courts or tribunals established under laws relating to the Armed Forces.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Original, Writ, Appellate, Supervisory. These represent the four main pillars of High Court jurisdiction.

exam_strategy_tips: Focus on Article 227 (Supervisory) vs. Article 226 (Writ); they are often confused in matching questions.
Remember that the salary of High Court judges is charged to the Consolidated Fund of the STATE, but their pension is charged to the Consolidated Fund of INDIA.
